abstract: Working memory depends on gamma oscillations generated across sensory and prefrontal cortices. In primary visual cortex (V1), stimulus-locked gamma oscillations encode stimulus information, while in prefrontal cortex (PFC), persistent gamma oscillations maintain this information after the stimulus is removed. In schizophrenia (SZ), gamma power is reduced in both V1 and PFC, consistent with deficits in sensory encoding and working memory maintenance. Both oscillation regimes arise from a canonical microcircuit involving pyramidal neurons (PNs) and parvalbumin-expressing interneurons (PVIs). Yet, whether the two regimes are similarly or differentially vulnerable to synaptic alterations within this circuit in SZ remains unknown. To investigate this question, we used a mean-field model of the PN-PVI circuit, in which the two regimes were distinguished by NMDA conductance values reflecting the difference in GluN2B expression between human PFC and V1. We then assessed three synaptic alterations quantified using molecular and structural proxies in postmortem SZ brains: lower excitatory inputs to PVIs (E→I), lower inhibitory inputs to PNs (I→E), and greater variability in E→I strength. Each alteration produced larger gamma power deficits in the persistent regime than in the stimulus-locked regime. Applied together, these alterations interacted synergistically to reduce gamma power, with the persistent regime exhibiting a more pronounced deficit. Bifurcation analyses revealed that this differential vulnerability arises from a wider margin of oscillatory stability in the stimulus-locked regime, and that reduced I→E strength additionally abolished the bistability required for the persistent regime. These findings predict that a larger magnitude of synaptic alteration is required to disrupt gamma oscillations in V1 than in PFC, consistent with postmortem reports of more severe alterations in V1 in SZ. Together, they establish a differential vulnerability model of cortical gamma oscillations in SZ, in which regional differences in oscillatory stability determine how much synaptic alteration is required to disrupt oscillations with distinct dynamics.
